1.text:
“Alif-Lãm-Mĩm-Ṣãd” opens the surah as disconnected letters. One gloss uses the phrase “God knows best what He means by these letters”; another gives the wording “I am Allah Who knows best” and also keeps an oath reading. Two other explanations point back to an earlier explanation of disconnected letters. They do not give a word for each letter; the meaning remains with God. An overview of the surah links its subjects to the return to the Hereafter and prophethood, then to past prophets and their communities, along with their reward and punishment. Another note frames the Book as guidance for the few and a warning to those moving toward a grievous fate. These are subjects of the surah, not explanations of the four opening letters. The comments provide context for the chapter while leaving the meaning of the letters with God, as one gloss puts it.

**The letters, their readings, and the oath.**

Alif Lām Mīm Sād God knows best what He means by these letters. I am Allah Who knows best and is best; it is also said that this is an oath by which Allah swore. This surah begins with the disconnected letters, the explanation for which has already preceded in Surah Baqarah. We mentioned before the explanation of the letters [such as, Alif-Lam, that are in the beginning of some Surahs in the Qur'an].

**The surah’s subjects across its sections.**

An overview of the Surah shows that most of the subjects it deals with are related to Ma ad (Return to the Hereafter) and Risalah (Prophethood). The former appear from the beginning of the Surah upto approximately the end of the sixth section. Then, from the eighth to the twenty first sections, there is a detailed description of past prophets, events about their communities, their reward and punishment and the punishment which overtook them.

**Guidance, warning, truth, and substance.**

The Book of God is, in essence, a book of guidance. But as such it is of value only to the few who have kept their consciences alive. For the others it amounts only to a warning of the impending grievous fate towards which they are moving because of their arrogance. The preacher of truth is concerned to see that what he sees as the absolute truth is being rejected by the majority of the people who consider it a falsehood. What is paramount in his eyes is treated by people with unconcern, as if it had no substance, as if it were completely unreal.

2.text:
The verse first names what has been sent down: “This is a Book sent down to you, O Prophet.” The wording places the Book before the strain of carrying it, so its origin and its task are clear before the difficulty is named. “Do not let anxiety into your heart regarding it” speaks to the inner burden that can accompany a message rejected by its hearers. It does not change what the Book is or what it asks; it tells the Prophet not to be held back by the pressure around its delivery. The next words, “so with it you may warn the disbelievers,” give that delivery a purpose: the warning is carried through the Book, not made up apart from it. “And as a reminder to the believers” turns to another audience. The same Book warns those who reject it and renews the attention of those who believe. The line therefore joins reassurance with responsibility: the Prophet is not asked to control every response, but he is given a clear message to convey. Its closing phrase prepares for the next command, which tells people to follow what has been sent down and not to turn to other protectors. The emphasis is not on anxiety by itself, but on what the revealed words are for and how different hearers meet them. For those already believing, a reminder is useful because it brings the message back to mind; for those refusing it, the warning makes the consequence plain. Both purposes belong to the same Book. The letters at the start of the surah are followed by the plain name of the Book here, and the next verse turns from its purpose to the duty of following it.

**The revealed Book.**

This is a Book that is revealed to you — addressing the Prophet s — so let there be no inhibition no constraint in your breast because of it to convey it — for fear that you might be called a liar — that you may warn thereby li-tundhira ‘that you may warn’ is semantically connected to unzila ‘is revealed’ that is to say ‘it is revealed for the purposes of warning’ and as a reminder for those who believe in it. ((It is) a Scripture) this Scripture, i.e. the Qur'an (that is revealed unto thee (Muhammad) that Gabriel brought to you (so let there be no heaviness in thy heart) let there be no doubt in your heart (therefrom) i.e. there can be no doubt about the Qur'an being from Allah (that thou mayst warn thereby) that you may warn the people of Makkah through the Qur'an in order that they believe, (and (it is) a Reminder unto believers).

**The burden in the heart.**

Some commentators have said that haraj' or constraint on the heart' refers to the constraint experienced by the Holy Prophet who, because of his affectionate concern for people, felt pain when they would not believe despite having heard the Qur'an and its injunctions. To offset this constraint, the Holy Prophet has been told that the duty with which he has been obligated is simply to make the call and convey the message. (haraj) translated here as constraint' means that you should have no anguish or apprehension in conveying the Qur'an and its injunctions lest people belie it and hurt you.' (As reported from Abu Al- Aliyah - Mazhari) The hint given here is that Allah who has sent down this Book on you has also made arrangements that you shall remain protected and that takes care of any anguish on your part. The noble Qur’ān is a scripture revealed by Allah to you, O Prophet, so do not let there be any distress or doubt in your heart about it.

**The warning, truth, and substance.**

For the others it amounts only to a warning of the impending grievous fate towards which they are moving because of their arrogance. The preacher of truth is concerned to see that what he sees as the absolute truth is being rejected by the majority of the people who consider it a falsehood. What is paramount in his eyes is treated by people with unconcern, as if it had no substance, as if it were completely unreal. He revealed it to you to warn people by it and to be a proof, and to remind those who have faith through it, because it is they who benefit from being reminded.

3.text:
After naming the Book and its purpose, the verse turns from what was sent down to what people are to do with it. “Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord” makes the direction plain: the guidance is not something to be set aside when another voice is easier. “And do not take others as guardians besides Him” marks the alternative the verse refuses, a turn toward other protectors in place of the Lord. The command is not just to hear the words, but to keep to them, and the second phrase prevents a divided loyalty. “How seldom are you mindful” closes with a rebuke about remembering. It asks why people who have been shown what was sent down still act as if they had forgotten it. The verse links revelation to choice: people may accept or reject the message during their lives, yet the reminder calls them to bring what they know into their decisions now. It also moves the passage forward. The preceding verse described the Book as both warning and reminder; this verse explains the response expected from its hearers. The next verses turn to communities that failed to respond, showing that what is neglected in life does not disappear from the account. So the command to follow stands between a message given and the consequences of how people answer it. The verse speaks to all who hear, not just to the person first addressed, and it does not allow the hearer to treat another protector as a substitute for the instruction already sent down. Its closing words return to memory, making recollection practical in the choices that follow. The first phrase gives the direction, the next names what is to be left aside, and the last returns to memory. Read in order, the verse moves from revelation to obedience and then to the rebuke for forgetting. It does not leave the hearer with memory alone, because the command to follow comes before the words about remembering. The wording places other protectors besides the Lord and tells the hearer not to follow them. The warning and reminder in the verse before this one now become a direction for conduct.

**Following what was sent down.**

Say to them Follow what has been revealed to you from your Lord namely the Qur’ān and do not follow do not take beside Him namely God in other words other than Him any patrons obeying them in disobedience of Him exalted be He. ((Saying): Follow that which is sent down unto you from your Lord) i.e. the Qur'an: uphold as lawful that which it makes lawful and unlawful that which it makes unlawful, (and follow) and worship (no protecting friends) idols as lords (beside Him. Little do you recollect) you do not take admonition neither much nor a little! (Follow what has been sent down unto you from your Lord) meaning, follow and imitate the unlettered Prophet , who brought you a Book that was revealed for you, from the Lord and master of everything.

**Following other protectors.**

(and follow not any Awliya', besides Him (Allah) meaning, do not disregard what the Messenger brought you and follow something else, for in this case, you will be deviating from Allah's judgment to the decision of someone else. Do not follow the desires of those you imagine to be friends and protectors amongst the devils or evil scholars, turning to them and leaving what was revealed to you because of your desires.

**Remembering, rejection, and truth.**

Little do you remember read tadhakkarūn or yadhakkarūn ‘little are you or they admonished’; the original tā’ of tatadhakkarūn has been assimilated with the dhāl; a variant reading has tadhkurūn; the mā of qalīlan mā ‘little’ is extra merely emphasising the ‘littleness’. Here everybody has the opportunity and the liberty to accept or reject the truth as he pleases, and even find clever words to justify his stand. As soon as the period of trial comes to an end, it will be revealed to all that the preacher’s words were based on eternal truths; that it was sheer bias and egotism on his opponents’ part which prevented them from seeing the Truth at the core of his arguments. It will become clear at that time that the arguments advanced by them to contradict the preacher’s words were simply a falsification of the facts and not a form of reasoning in any real sense. If you had remembered, you would not have preferred falsehood over the truth, and you would have followed what your Messenger came with, acting in obedience to it and leaving anything besides it.

4.text:
The verse opens by making the number of destroyed societies a question that points beyond any one town: “Imagine, how many societies We have destroyed!” It turns the listener toward repeated examples, not a single unexpected event. “Our torment took them by surprise, while sleeping, at night or midday” explains the turn. The communities did not take command of the moment or choose when to face it; the arrival is pictured as sudden. The final phrase sets two ordinary times side by side. Night is when people rest, while midday can also be a time of rest, so the warning reaches into hours when no one expects to be confronted. The verse does not describe a defense or a rescue by the powers they trusted. It brings the outcome forward and lets the next line give the words left to those who were overcome. The previous verses call the hearer to follow what was sent down and remind them of the result of refusing guidance. This verse makes that result visible through earlier societies, and the following verse gives their own short admission. The sequence moves from warning, to sudden punishment, to the confession that follows. In this way the question about how many is not a count to be worked out, but an invitation to think about how often a people has met the same end while feeling secure. The two times of day make the surprise plain, and the word societies broadens the lesson beyond one group. The sudden arrival matters because the people are shown at rest, not preparing to meet what comes. The two times do not set an hour for the hearer to expect; they show that punishment came both at night and in the middle of the day. A town’s confidence did not keep it safe. The number in the opening question remains broad, because the warning concerns a repeated outcome, not one group alone. The next line gives the words the people had left when that outcome reached them. The rest at night and midday makes the surprise part of the account rather than a detail about a single place.

**The number of destroyed towns.**

How many kam is predicative and is the direct object of the main verb ahlaknāhā ‘We have destroyed’ a city meaning its inhabitants have We destroyed have We willed its destruction! (How many a township) people of townships (have We destroyed) We tormented! How many cities Allah has destroyed through His punishment because they persisted in their disbelief and error! (And many a township did We destroy while they were given to wrongdoing, so that it lie in ruins (up to this day), and (many) a deserted well and lofty castle!)[22:45], and,.

**The night and the midday rest.**

So Our might Our chastisement came upon it at night or while they slept at noon qā’ilūn al-qaylūla is a rest taken halfway during the day even if it does not involve sleep in other words sometimes it came upon it at night and sometimes it came during the day. (Our torment came upon them by night or while they were taking their midday nap.) means, Allah's command, torment and vengeance came over them at night or while taking a nap in the middle of the day. Both of these times are periods of rest and leisure or heedlessness and amusement. (As a raid by night) or day, (or while they slept at noon, Our terror) Our punishment (came unto them). Allah sent His punishment down on them in their obliviousness at night or during the day: they could not do anything to avoid the punishment, and their false gods could do nothing to protect them from it.

**The world, truth, and untruth.**

In this world the importance of an individual is gauged by the material splendour surrounding him, and his ability to influence people with his impressive words, and thus have a massive following. Since the preacher is not generally in such a happy position, his word is valueless in the eyes of worldly people, while the words of his opponents, who bask in material grandeur have a greater impact. But when Doomsday uncovers all the facts, the position will be just the opposite. Now, all the weight will be on the side of the Truth: Untruth will be divested of all its arguments and will be rendered valueless.

5.text:
The line moves from the sudden arrival of the punishment to what its hearers could say afterward. “Their only cry” narrows the response to one statement, with no other plea placed beside it. “When overwhelmed by Our torment, was” locates that statement at the moment the punishment reaches them, not earlier when a warning could still be acted on. “We have indeed been wrongdoers” is the confession itself. They do not speak of a lack of signs or of another power that could protect them. The verse leaves the confession short, and the previous line explains why it comes only after the torment has arrived. The people now name their own wrong, but the words do not undo what has happened. In the surrounding passage, the Book has already been presented as warning and reminder, and the command was to follow what was sent down. This verse gives the consequence of ignoring that command from the side of those who are overtaken. The next line widens the account by placing both the communities and the messengers before questioning. The admission therefore belongs to a larger reckoning, where what was done and how the message was received are brought into view. The confession is brief because the line leaves no second plea beside it. Maʿārif’s earlier note concerns the Prophet’s pain when people heard the Qur’an and would not believe; here the same rejection reaches the moment of admitted wrong.

**The plea when the torment came.**

And their only plea their only words when Our might came upon them was to say ‘We were evildoers indeed’. (No cry did they utter when Our torment came upon them but this: "Verily, we were wrongdoers.") (No plea) words (had they, when Our terror) Our punishment which destroyed them (came unto them, save that they said: Lo! We were wrong-doers) idolaters. This means, when the torment came to them, their cry was that they admitted their sins and that they deserved to be punished.

**The wrong they admitted.**

(No plea) words (had they, when Our terror) Our punishment which destroyed them (came unto them, save that they said: Lo! We were wrong-doers) idolaters. All they could do when the punishment came down on them was to admit that they had done wrong through their disbelief in Allah. This means, when the torment came to them, their cry was that they admitted their sins and that they deserved to be punished.

**The plea at the time of torment.**

And their only plea their only words when Our might came upon them was to say ‘We were evildoers indeed’. (No plea) words (had they, when Our terror) Our punishment which destroyed them (came unto them, save that they said: Lo! We were wrong-doers) idolaters. (No cry did they utter when Our torment came upon them but this: "Verily, we were wrongdoers.") This means, when the torment came to them, their cry was that they admitted their sins and that they deserved to be punished.

To offset this constraint, the Holy Prophet has been told that the duty with which he has been obligated is simply to make the call and convey the message.

6.text:
The verse places two groups before a future questioning: “We will surely question those who received messengers and We will question the messengers themselves.” The first phrase points to the people who heard a message and must answer for how they received it. The second turns the question toward those who carried the message, so the record includes both the hearers and the ones sent to them. “We will surely question” is repeated in the meaning even as the subjects change, giving each group its own responsibility. The verse follows the account of communities that admitted wrongdoing only after punishment arrived. It now looks beyond that moment to the day when their response to messengers will be examined. At the same time, it does not collapse the two questions into one: people answer for their response, while messengers answer for conveying what they were sent with. The next verse promises a full account with knowledge, and that none of this happened in absence. So this line begins the scene of questioning, rather than giving every detail of the answers. The repeated question makes clear that the message and its reception both matter, while keeping the duty of the hearer distinct from the duty of the one sent.

**People and messengers before questioning.**

We shall question these people about their response to the messengers, (and verily We shall question the messengers) about their conveyance of the message. Allah will certainly question the communities He sent messengers to on the Day of Judgement: about how they received the messengers. Allah will question the nations, on the Day of Resurrection, how they responded to His Messengers and the Messages He sent them with.

**The messengers and their delivery.**

Then verily We shall question those to whom the Message was sent that is We shall question those communities about their response to the messengers and to what extent they implemented that which was conveyed to them; and We shall question the messengers about the conveying of that Message. He will also question the Messengers if they conveyed His Messages.

**The messengers and the questions asked.**

The statement: ‌ ‌ 6 in verse 6 refers to the day of Qiyamah when people will be asked by Allah how did they receive the messengers and Books sent to them by Him - and the messengers will be asked if they did convey to their communities the message and injunctions Allah had sent them with. Also, He will certainly question the messengers about whether they delivered what they were instructed to deliver, and how their communities responded to it.

7.text:
After saying that both the communities and the messengers will be questioned, the verse explains how the account will be given. “Then We will give them a full account with sure knowledge” points to a complete telling of what they did, not a partial recollection. This complete telling is not based on guesswork or on a report that might have been missed. The final phrase, “for We were never absent,” gives the reason the account can be complete: nothing was outside the knowledge of the One who was present when the messengers conveyed the message and when the people responded. The verse's order matters. It first promises a full account, then names the knowledge behind it, and closes by removing the possibility that some action escaped notice. The preceding verse asks both audiences about their part, while this one brings their whole story forward. The next verses describe the scales and the differing outcomes, so the account leads into a just weighing rather than ending with questioning alone. The line also answers any thought that an unseen or private action would be missing: what was done in public and what was hidden belongs to the same account. This is why the verse pairs a full telling with constant knowledge, and why the lack of absence is its final point. Neither time nor place could put a person's conduct beyond the account. The full telling is not just a list; it is an exact account of what was done.

**Knowledge and the facts brought to light.**

(Then verily We shall narrate unto them) inform them (with knowledge) with elucidation, (for verily We were not absent) from the conveyance of the messengers and the response of the people (when it came to pass). Allah will inform everyone about what they did in the world, through His knowledge, because He was always aware of whatever they did. But when Doomsday uncovers all the facts, the position will be just the opposite.

**The communities and messengers in the question.**

The statement: ‌ ‌ 6 in verse 6 refers to the day of Qiyamah when people will be asked by Allah how did they receive the messengers and Books sent to them by Him - and the messengers will be asked if they did convey to their communities the message and injunctions Allah had sent them with. Allah will question the nations, on the Day of Resurrection, how they responded to His Messengers and the Messages He sent them with.

**Nothing was absent from the account.**

(Then surely, We shall narrate unto them (their whole story) with knowledge, and indeed We have not been absent.) "The Book will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection and it will speak, disclosing what they used to do." Nothing is hidden from Him, and He was never, at any point, absent from them. (and indeed We have not been absent) meaning, On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will inform His servants about what they said and did, whether substantial or minor.

**Worldly judgment and the final truth.**

In this world the importance of an individual is gauged by the material splendour surrounding him, and his ability to influence people with his impressive words, and thus have a massive following. Since the preacher is not generally in such a happy position, his word is valueless in the eyes of worldly people, while the words of his opponents, who bask in material grandeur have a greater impact. Now, all the weight will be on the side of the Truth: Untruth will be divested of all its arguments and will be rendered valueless.

8.text:
This verse shifts from the full account to the measure by which deeds will be weighed. “The weighing on that Day will be just” states the standard before it names either outcome; no person is treated unfairly. “As for those whose scale will be heavy with good deeds” introduces one side of the result. The wording identifies what makes it heavy. “Only they will be successful” closes by naming success as the outcome for those whose deeds outweigh the other side. The line does not describe success as worldly status or as having more possessions. Its measure belongs to the Day when the whole account has been given. It follows the promise that every community and messenger will be questioned and that nothing was absent from the account. It then prepares for the next verse, which names the opposite scale and gives the light scale’s outcome. The two verses are placed together so that the justice of the weighing is heard before either result is described. The heavy scale is not a claim that a person was without fault; it is the stated side of a just comparison, with good deeds carrying weight. The phrase “on that Day” points back to the questioning and the full account, so the scale is part of one process. The ending does not leave the reader with a bare measurement; it names success as the result for those whose deeds weigh more. The verse gives the standard first, then moves from that standard to the first result, leaving the next line to state the other.

**A just weighing.**

The weighing of deeds or of the scrolls of these deeds shall be — in a balance that has a tongue and two palms as scales as reported in a hadīth — on that day that is on the day of the questioning mentioned namely the Day of Resurrection the true weighing the fair weighing al-haqq ‘the true’ is an adjectival qualification of al-wazn ‘the weighing’. Here, the hint given is that let no one be deceived by the idea that things which usually get to be weighed or measured are things having some weight or heaviness. Human deeds, good or bad, have no body or mass which could be weighed. (And the Weighing on that day is definite) so that man, all infatuated with the obvious, may not be able to deny the weighing of deeds in the Hereafter - which stands proved from the Holy Qur'an and is the collective belief of the Muslim Ummah. The weighing of what they did on the Day of Judgement will be with justice, with no one being wronged in the least.

**The things that are weighed.**

As for what will be placed on the Balance on the Day of Resurrection, it has been said that the deeds will be placed on it, even though they are not material objects. Allah will give these deeds physical weight on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said that the Book of Records that contains the deeds will be weighed. A Hadith states that a man will be brought forth and ninety-nine scrolls containing errors and sins will be placed on one side of the balance each as long as the sight can reach. It is also possible to combine the meanings of these Ayat and Hadiths by stating that all this will truly occur, for sometimes the deeds will be weighed, sometimes the scrolls where they are recorded will be weighed, and sometimes those who performed the deeds will be weighed. Now, if Allah Almighty, the Maker of makers, in His perfect power, could weigh or measure human deeds - with or without a device - what is there in it which would make it to be something far out to believe? Leaving this aside for a moment, the Creator of the Universe does have the power to transform our deeds at some time into a material presence, even give it some shape or form (interesting that people would believe something like this happening in a Speilberg movie, yet squirm at the religious view of things as would come to pass).

**Heavy scales and the inward state.**

So, as for those whose scale (of good deeds) will be heavy, they will be the successful (by entering Paradise)And as for those whose scale will be light, they are those who will lose themselves for their wrongful behavior with Our Ayat. Those whose good actions weigh more than their bad actions have succeeded in reaching the goal and being saved from what they feared. The one whose scale-pan with good deeds is heavier will have his salvation while the one whose scale-pan with sins and evils is heavier will have his punishment. The weighing of deeds with the scales of self-purification is true, and the weighing of states with the scales of truthfulness is just. Hapless and deprived is he whose deeds are tainted with eye service and whose states are mixed with self-admiration, for in the station of the scales these states will have no value and those deeds will have no weight.

9.text:
The next line gives the other side of the weighing. “But those whose scale is light” turns from the successful to those whose deeds do not carry enough weight, and the contrast is signaled by the opening word. “They have doomed themselves for wrongfully denying Our signs” puts the loss on the people themselves; it is not described as a loss imposed without a reason. The ending names the action connected to that loss. The verse therefore does not leave the light scale as an unexplained result; it links it to denial. It follows the statement that the weighing is just, so the contrast between the scales is part of the same fair reckoning. The previous verse names success for those whose scale is heavy, and this verse names the self-loss of the other group. Together they set out two outcomes, not as a guess about anyone's present standing, but as a final result at the weighing. The next verses return from the Day of Judgment to the favors given in this world and the many who give little thanks; the contrast asks readers to notice how they respond before their deeds are weighed. The word “signs” gathers the message they had rejected, not one isolated mark. The scale is light because their actions and their denial meet in the same result, while the earlier line has named success on the other side.

**The light scale and its result.**

And as for those whose scales are light because of evil deeds those are the ones who have lost their souls by causing them to travel towards the Fire because they mistreated they knowingly denied Our signs. So, as for those whose scale (of good deeds) will be heavy, they will be the successful (by entering Paradise)And as for those whose scale will be light, they are those who will lose themselves for their wrongful behavior with Our Ayat.

**Those who lose themselves.**

(those are they who lose their souls) by being punished (because they disbelieved Our revelations) Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an. Those whose bad actions weigh more than their good actions are the people who have lost themselves, gaining their destruction on the Day of Judgement and being excluded from eternal bliss because of their rejection of Allah’s signs and verses. In the two verses the Tafsir of which you have just read through, sinners were warned against the disgrace on the plain of Resurrection and the Divine punishment that would come in its wake.

**Worldly standing, truth, and untruth.**

In this world the importance of an individual is gauged by the material splendour surrounding him, and his ability to influence people with his impressive words, and thus have a massive following. Since the preacher is not generally in such a happy position, his word is valueless in the eyes of worldly people, while the words of his opponents, who bask in material grandeur have a greater impact. But when Doomsday uncovers all the facts, the position will be just the opposite. Now, all the weight will be on the side of the Truth: Untruth will be divested of all its arguments and will be rendered valueless.

10.text:
The verse returns from the weighing to the life people now live. “We have indeed established you on earth and provided you with a means of livelihood” names the place where human life is set and what is needed to live there. The two phrases belong together: a place to live is accompanied by ways to seek food, drink, clothing, work, and other needs. The verse then marks the response with “Yet,” turning from what has been given to what people give back. “Yet you seldom give any thanks” does not deny that people receive these provisions; it shows their gratitude is small beside what they have received. The first-person wording keeps the gifts tied to their giver, while the closing phrase makes human forgetfulness the concern. The previous two verses described the scales of deeds on the Day of Judgment. This verse moves to present life and asks the reader to notice what choices are being made now, before the accounting. The following verses begin the story of Adam and Satan, which continues the warning about disobedience and ingratitude. So the line is both a reminder of provision and a test of how people respond to it. Its words do not limit livelihood to one kind of work or one kind of possession, but point to what sustains a life on earth. The final turn is not a small detail. It makes thanks the question raised by the verse and by the human story that follows.

**The earth and its comfort.**

Then comes the third verse which mentions the blessings of Allah Ta ala and persuades people to accept truth and act accordingly by suggesting that Allah has bestowed on them full ownership and control on the earth and has opened thousands of avenues of comfort for them. It is as if the Master of the Universe has made this whole earth and what it contains a giant warehouse of human needs and comforts, a most compre-hensive inventory of that inside it.

**Livelihood and life on earth.**

And We have given you power O Children of Adam in the earth and have appointed for you therein livelihoods ma‘āyish is the plural of ma‘īsha that is the means by which you are able to subsist; little qalīlan mā mā is to emphasise the ‘littleness’ thanks you show for this. (And We have given you (mankind) power in the earth, and appointed for you therein) in the earth (a livelihood) that from which you eat, drink and clothe yourselves. Allah certainly established you, O children of Adam, on the earth, and gave you the means of making a living.

**Sustenance and benefits.**

Allah reminds of His favor on His servants in that He made the earth a fixed place for dwelling, placed firm mountains and rivers on it and made homes and allowed them to utilize its benefits. Allah made the clouds work for them (bringing rain) so that they may produce their sustenance from them. He also created the ways and means of earnings, commercial activities and other professions. One who is short on sense and manners and does not know how to take things out from this warehouse, or does not understand how to use what he has taken out, he remains deprived of their benefits.

**Gratitude and forgetfulness.**

Whatever God has bestowed upon man in this world has been given for the purpose of eliciting his gratitude. But this is the very thing which man does not offer to his Lord. The reason for this is that Satan contrives to distort his feelings and steers him away from any expression of gratitude. You should be thankful to Allah for that, but you give little thanks. In short, Allah Ta ala has placed all that human beings need on and in this earth which demands that they should be grateful to Him all the time under all conditions. They would not take much time to forget the favours of their Creator and Master - only to return to the same world of things. So, at the end of the verse, it is in a mode of complaint that it was said: ‌ (Little you are receptive to advice).
